title: Connotation: making associations
subtitle: a dove, a hawk, a real diamond, cowboy builders
summary: Read between the lines of English words: the associations that dove, hawk, shark, diamond, colours and animals carry, and why journalists and advertisers use them.

lesson.heading: Words carry associations
lesson.text: We often **associate** words with something that is not obvious from their literal meaning. The **dove** is a white bird that has associations with peace, so a journalist who calls a politician a **dove** is suggesting that he or she is a peacemaker. A more aggressive, hard-line politician is a **hawk** - a bird which hunts its prey.

examples.text: The prime minister is a **dove** on foreign policy, but his deputy is a **hawk**.
Associations like these are shared by most speakers of English and may even be listed in a good learner's dictionary.

lesson.heading: Shared, regional and personal associations
lesson.text: Some associations vary from one geographical area to another: **black cats** have associations with good luck in Britain but with bad luck in the USA. Many associations are purely personal - someone who had a bad experience of dogs in childhood may think of a dog as fierce and frightening, while for others dogs represent loyalty and friendship.

examples.text: The most commonly shared association of the word **dog** in English is faithfulness.
But **a dog's life** refers to a very unhappy and unpleasant life.

lesson.note: Research shows that words are better remembered if you have personal associations in mind as you learn them.

lesson.heading: How writers use associations
lesson.text: Journalists, advertisers and other writers use word associations to interest and entertain their audience. A fashion advert might ask whether you would like that **Paris look**, drawing on the association of Paris with glamour and style. And **cowboy builders** are builders who are not careful or trustworthy - the association comes from the careless, dishonest cowboys of Westerns.

examples.text: Would you like to have that **Paris look**?
We had our kitchen ruined by **cowboy** plumbers.

lesson.heading: Working out what the speaker means
rows: a large sea creature with sharp teeth
the speaker does not like the garage - the people there are aggressive and dishonest
That new office block is a **scar** on the landscape.
a mark left on the skin after a cut has healed
the speaker thinks it spoils something that was once unspoilt
the speaker has a very high opinion of Emma
lesson.note: Your knowledge of the world and of the word's primary meaning is usually enough to decode the association.

lesson.heading: Colours and their associations in English
rows: purple was the colour of royal robes and of the most important Romans' togas
green is the colour of new growth
the colour skin may go when someone is afraid
red is the colour of fire
white is the absence of colour, a blank sheet
darkness suggests things hidden and frightening

lesson.heading: Animals and their associations
rows: a dog is totally under the control of its master
many people fear snakes and know they can be dangerous
light brown and not especially striking
a mouse is light brown or grey and not a popular animal
rats have very unpleasant associations for most English speakers
tend to say unkind things about people
cats have sharp claws that scratch and hurt
fish can smell unpleasant, and a smell makes you ask what is causing it
they just follow others, with no independence
sheep follow one another rather than acting alone
as a bird of prey, the hawk needs very sharp sight

lesson.heading: Good luck and bad luck in Britain
rows: good luck in Britain, bad luck in the USA

lesson.text: When a word is used oddly, ask what the thing it names is actually like - the answer is usually the connotation the speaker intends.

exercises.statement: You would happily recommend a cowboy plumber to a friend.
exercises.explanation: No - cowboy builders and plumbers are careless and not trustworthy.

exercises.prompt: A politician would be more likely to be called a dove if they ___.
exercises.explanation: The dove is associated with peace; the hawk with aggression.

exercises.prompt: Which is more likely to be called a scar on the landscape?
exercises.explanation: A scar is the mark of a wound on something that was once unspoilt.

exercises.statement: You would be pleased to be called a diamond.
exercises.explanation: Correct - a diamond is beautiful and valuable, so it is a compliment.

exercises.statement: Supersharks would be a good name for a business.
exercises.explanation: No - although super suggests something extra good, shark has a negative meaning in a business context.

exercises.prompt: Match each colour with its association in English.

exercises.statement: If you say someone has a dog's life, you think they have an easy life.
exercises.explanation: If you say someone has a dog's life, you think they have a difficult life.

exercises.statement: If you call a businessman a snake, you trust him.
exercises.explanation: If you call a businessman a snake, you do not trust him.

exercises.statement: If you say someone is being ratty, you mean they are irritable.
exercises.explanation: Correct - rats have unpleasant associations, so rattiness is a negative quality.

exercises.statement: If you say something is fishy, you mean it is suspicious.
exercises.explanation: Correct - an unpleasant smell makes you ask what is causing it.

exercises.prompt: If you say someone's hair is mousy, you mean it is ___.
options: light brown and not especially striking
exercises.explanation: A mouse is light brown or grey, so mousy has dull associations.

exercises.prompt: If you say someone can be catty, you mean they ___.
options: tend to say unkind things about people
exercises.explanation: Cats have sharp claws that scratch, so catty remarks hurt.

exercises.prompt: If you call someone a sheep, you mean they ___.
options: just follow others and are not independent
exercises.explanation: Sheep follow one another rather than acting independently.

exercises.prompt: If you say that someone is hawk-eyed, you mean that they ___.
exercises.explanation: As a bird of prey, the hawk needs very sharp sight.

exercises.prompt: In Britain, does each sign mean good luck or bad luck?
They're all ___ in that garage - they charged me twice what the repair was worth.
exercises.explanation: Shark suggests aggressive, dishonest behaviour, especially in business.

exercises.prompt: Emma's a real ___. She helped me every single day when I was ill.
exercises.explanation: Calling someone a diamond shows a very high opinion of them.

exercises.prompt: Put this advertising line in order.
exercises.answer: Would you like to have that Paris look?
exercises.explanation: The advert draws on the association of Paris with glamour and style.
